transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

Probably not. A loud hum/buzz from an induction hob with a large stockpot on high power is often normal, especially on Boost/max settings.

Common harmless causes:
• High power / PowerBoost: induction coils switch at high frequency and can become audible at maximum output.
• Large or thin-based stockpot: the base can vibrate slightly in the magnetic field, producing a buzz, hum, or rattling sound.
• Pan construction: multi-layer bases, slightly warped bases, loose handles, or a lid can resonate more than other cookware.
• Power sharing: if other zones are running, the hob may cycle power between zones, changing the noise.

Things to try:
1. Reduce the setting one or two levels from maximum/Boost. If the noise drops markedly, it is likely normal induction noise.
2. Try the same zone with another large, flat, induction-compatible pan.
3. Check that the pot base is clean, dry, flat, and centred on the marked zone.
4. Remove or steady the lid—sometimes it is the lid/handle rather than the hob.
5. Don’t run a large pot empty on high power.

Arrange service or stop using it if the noise is accompanied by any of these:
• burning smell, smoke, sparking, or repeated tripping of the breaker;
• an error code, failure to heat properly, or the hob switching itself off unexpectedly;
• a new harsh grinding/clicking noise even with no pan present;
• a cracked glass surface;
• noise that remains unusually loud at low settings with several different suitable pans.

If it only happens with that stockpot at high power and cooking otherwise works normally, it is very unlikely to mean the Bosch PUE611BB1E is about to fail.

Thanks, that's reassuring. I tried a few of those: it's much quieter at 6 and below, and my heavy cast iron pot is quiet on the same zone. The new stockpot and a cheap frying pan both buzz though. There are no error codes and no burning smell, and it heats normally. Is the pan itself the likely cause?

Yes — based on that, the cookware is the likely cause rather than the hob.

The strong clues are:

• The noise reduces substantially below power level 6.
• A heavy cast-iron pot is quiet on the same zone.
• The hob heats normally and shows no faults.
• Two lighter/cheaper pans buzz, which suggests their bases are vibrating or resonating under the induction field.

Induction hobs can make certain pans’ magnetic base layers vibrate, particularly at high power. Lighter stainless stockpots and cheaper frying pans often have thinner bases, less rigid bonded layers, or slight unevenness, so they can act a bit like a speaker cone. It does not usually mean the pan is unsafe or defective.

You can keep using the stockpot if:

• it sits flat and stable;
• the base is not visibly bowed, loose, or delaminating;
• it heats evenly;
• there is no scorching, smell, or unusual discolouration; and
• the noise is just a hum/buzz rather than metallic scraping or violent rattling.

For quieter use, bring the contents up to heat on high if needed, then turn it down to around 6 or lower once boiling. Avoid Boost for long periods with a large, thin-bottomed pot. If you replace it, look for an induction stockpot with a thick, flat, fully encapsulated magnetic base; heavier multi-ply cookware generally tends to be quieter.
